title: Oileán na Naomh
subtitle: Island of Saints and Scholars — Cluain Mhic Nóis, c. 780 AD

sessions.en: Dawn at the scriptorium — the living present
sessions.hook: Tomorrow the hours begin to count. Murchadh will want you to say what time it is — and how many pages remain.

beats.n: The Shannon lies flat under mist. Somewhere across the water a bell rings — once, twice — and the monastery wakes in layers: sandalled feet on stone, a door on leather hinges, smoke from the kitchen drifting over the cloister.

You have travelled forward from Dáire's stone yard — centuries forward, east along the great river — and the work waiting for you here is not carved in rock but painted on vellum: a gospel book that must be finished before winter.
Candlelight still fights the grey. A man bent over a ruled page looks up without surprise, as if he had been expecting you since Matins.

beats.g: I am Murchadh — identity still takes *is*, not *tá*

beats.n: He gestures at the benches, the ink horns, the half-finished quires stacked like fallen leaves.

beats.s: Tá muid ag obair anseo gach lá.
beats.g: We are working here every day — *tá* for what is happening *now*
beats.ph: taw mwidj eg OH-bir un-YOH gokh law

pages.title: An Nóta Gramadaí — *Tá mé* and *Is mise*, at last
paras: In Chapter 1, Murchadh's distant cousin Dáire taught you **Is mise** — who someone *is*. That was identity: name, origin, the copula **is**.
**Tá** is the other “to be” — the one for *states and actions happening now*: working, writing, eating, tired, cold. Not who you are — what you are *doing* or *feeling*.
School often blurs them. From here on, ask: am I naming myself (*is*) or describing the moment (*tá*)?
pairs: Tá mé ag scríobh. — I am writing. (right now)
Tá mé tuirseach. — I am tired. (a state)

pages.context: Cillín, a younger monk, is copying a line at the next bench. He overhears and tries to help.
pages.prompt: He wants to say “I am Cillín.” Which is it?

opts.why: A name is identity → the copula. Is mise Cillín.
Tá is for states and actions — writing, tired, hungry. Being Cillín is not a passing condition.
Irish keeps its order here: Is mise Cillín.

pages.prompt: Murchadh is ruling vellum *right now*. How does he say “I am working”?

opts.why: An action in progress → tá + ag + verbal noun. Tá mé ag obair.
Is is for identity, not for what you're doing this minute.
The verb of being comes first: Tá mé ag obair.

beats.n: Murchadh sets a horn of ink within reach and names the day's verbs the way another man might name tools:

beats.s: Scríobh. Léigh. Meilt. Ith. Codail. Obair.
beats.g: Write. Read. Grind. Eat. Sleep. Work. — the scriptorium's daily round
beats.ph: shkreev · lay · melj · ih · KOD-il · OH-bir

beats.n: In the living present they become longer phrases:

beats.g: I am writing — literally ‘am I at writing’
Pangur Bán is eating — the white cat earns his keep

pages.title: An Nóta Gramadaí — the verb goes first (VSO)
paras: Watch the order: **Tá mé ag scríobh** — verb first, then *I*, then the action. Irish is **VSO**: Verb – Subject – Object.
English locks you into “I am writing.” Irish frees the verb to lead: the *doing* is what matters first. Questions work the same way — the verb still leads.
You don't need to memorise “VSO” as jargon. Just notice: Irish sentences often *start* with the action.
pairs: Tá mé ag scríobh. — Am-I at-writing. (I am writing.)
An bhfuil tú ag obair? — Are you at work? (Connacht; Munster often says An bhfuil tú ag obair? the same way; Ulster may use different question shapes later.)

pages.context: Cillín slides you a scrap of vellum to practise on.
pages.prompt: Build: “I am writing.”

pages.context: Murchadh listens without looking up — the scriptorium learns by ear first, always.
pages.g: I am writing — the shape you'll live in all week

pages.prompt: Match the phrase to its meaning.

beats.n: Cillín wipes ink from his fingers and grins — younger than his tonsure suggests. The scriptorium is small; everyone will know you by tomorrow, but introductions still matter.

beats.g: Who are you? — Connacht form (you'll also hear Cé thú? in other dialects)

pages.cue: Identity or action — both are true here. Pick the line that fits.

replies.g: I am {name} — leading with who you are

reaction.g: I know now — literally ‘there is knowledge at me’

reaction.n: He nods, satisfied. Names are still carved with **is**, even when the work is painted.

replies.g: I am working here — leading with what you're doing

reaction.g: We all are! — and that's the point

reaction.n: A laugh ripples down the benches. You chose *tá* — the living present — and the room answered in kind.

beats.n: The bell rings again — Lauds, and the day's count begins. Murchadh counts the stacked quires with his eyes.

beats.s: Tá sé ag éirí go mall.
beats.g: It is rising slowly — the sun, he means
beats.ph: taw shay eg AY-ree guh maul

beats.n: Tomorrow he'll teach you the hours by name — and how many pages stand between this dawn and winter.

sessions.en: The hours — counting pages and time
sessions.hook: Tomorrow the pigment sacks arrive from the west. You'll need every colour name before the winter ink runs dry.

pages.intro: You climb the scriptorium stairs past yesterday's practice sheet — vellum weathers faster than stone, but the wind gets at chalk all the same.

items.en: I am writing — yesterday's living present
I am… — identity, from Dáire's yard and Cillín's question

beats.n: Murchadh has ruled fresh pages overnight. He taps the margin with a stylus.

beats.s: Tá sé a sé a chlog.
beats.g: It is six o'clock — time counted aloud in the scriptorium
beats.ph: taw shay ah shay ah khlog

beats.n: He holds up fingers as he counts — not decoration, but how the house keeps account:

pages.title: Numbers that keep the book honest
paras: A gospel book is counted in **leathanaigh** — pages — and **cóipleabhair** — quires. Murchadh tracks both because winter doesn't negotiate.
**Aon** through **deich** will follow you into market haggling in a later century. For now they measure candles, pages, and the brothers at table.

pages.prompt: Match the number to its figure.

pages.context: Cillín asks how many quires remain.
pages.prompt: Murchadh says there are seven. Which word is “seven”?

opts.why: Seacht = seven. You'll hear it in prayers, pages, and head counts.
Sé = six — close in sound, but one short of seven.
Naoi = nine. Count again: seacht.

pages.prompt: Build: “It is three o'clock.”
pages.answer: Tá sé a trí a chlog

pages.title: The day's frame — monastic time in plain Irish
paras: The full liturgical cycle has many names — **Prím**, **Téire**, **Nóin**, **Vespers** — but daily speech uses the sky:
**Madainn** — morning. **Meán lae** — midday. **Tráthnóna** — evening.
All of them sit inside **tá sé…** — *it is…* — the same frame as the clock.
pairs: Tá sé moch sa mhaidin. — It is early in the morning.
Tá sé in am lóin. — It is lunchtime.
Tá sé déanach. — It is late.

parts.en: son of Nós — the saint who founded this place

pages.meaning: the meadow of the sons of Nós
pages.note: The English name kept the sound and dropped the meadow. From here the Shannon carried books and scholars outward — the *oileán na naomh* was never one island, but a network of places like this.

pages.context: Murchadh turns his back — count with your ear.
pages.prompt: Éist — which number did he say?

opts.why: The hard c and the ú — cúig. Five quires, five candles, five fingers extended.
Fifteen is cúig déag — you'll meet that form later. This was the plain five: cúig.
Ceithre ends softer. Cúig carries a longer ú.

pages.context: Cillín chalks the time wrong on a practice board: “Ta se a naoi a chlog.”
pages.prompt: Correct it — mind the fadas and *tá sé*.
pages.placeholder: Tá sé a naoi a chlog
pages.answer: Tá sé a naoi a chlog
pages.hint: Tá sé — two words, both with fadas.

pages.prompt: Which sentence says “It is late”?

opts.why: Déanach = late. Tá sé déanach — the day running out.
Late is a state of the time, not an identity. Tá sé déanach.
That would mean “I am ten” — true for fingers, not for the hour.

beats.n: At the window Murchadh watches a boat land below the round tower — sacks of colour, freighted from the west.
“Tomorrow,” he says, “you'll learn what those sacks cost — and what names the colours answer to.”

sessions.hook: Tomorrow is a fast day — but the refectory still has opinions, and Pangur Bán has his.

pages.intro: The pigment boat is unloading. On your way down you pass yesterday's hour-mark — the chalk already flaking.

items.answer: Tá sé a sé a chlog
items.en: it is six o'clock — how the day opened

pages.place: Seomra na ndath — the pigment room

beats.n: Mortars, pestles, sacks of unfamiliar smell. Murchadh unwraps a cake of purple matter the colour of winter dusk.

beats.s: Tá mé ag meilt an corcra.
beats.g: I am grinding the purple — corcra, from lichen that only grows on certain rocks
beats.ph: taw may eg melj un KOR-kruh

beats.n: He points along the bench — a row of horns like a rainbow caught in leather:

beats.s: Corcra. Gorm. Dearg. Buí. Dubh. Bán.
beats.g: Purple. Blue. Red. Yellow. Black. White.
beats.ph: KOR-kruh · GOR-um · JAR-ug · bwee · duv · bawn

pages.title: An Nóta Gramadaí — VSO in plain sight
paras: Look at **Tá mé ag meilt an corcra** — verb first, as always with *tá*.
Now shift to habit: **Scríobhann Cillín** — *writes Cillín* — verb first again, but this time the verb itself carries the present: *scríobhann* = writes/is writing.
Two present shapes, one freedom: **the verb leads**. Subject after. Object last. English puts *I* first; Irish puts *doing* first.
pairs: Itheann Pangur Bán. — Pangur Bán eats.
Léann Cillín an psalm. — Cillín reads the psalm.

pages.prompt: Match the colour to its ink.
pairs: purple — lichen purple, costly as praise
black — iron gall, the everyday line

pages.prompt: Which colour comes from woad — the blue?

opts.why: Gorm is blue in modern Irish — sky, water, woad in the horn.
Glas often means green — grass and growing things. The woad horn is gorm.
Buí is yellow — orpiment and sunlight. Not the blue.

pages.prompt: Build: “Cillín is writing.”

pages.context: Say the line that names the costliest colour.
pages.g: It is purple — identity again, for the ink itself

pages.prompt: Put the words in the order Irish expects: “Murchadh reads.”

opts.why: Verb first: Léann Murchadh. The reader follows the reading.
English order — understandable, but Irish wants the verb to lead.
Tá needs ag + verbal noun for progressive reading. Habitual present: Léann Murchadh.

pages.context: Cillín murmurs while he works — listen for the colour.
pages.prompt: Which word did he say?

opts.why: Dearg — the red lead in the margin rubrics.
Dubh is darker, flatter. Dearg carries the r against the teeth.
Bán is open and bright — vellum bare. He said dearg.

pages.caption: Every gospel opens with a capital — the *initium* — painted in corcra and gorm before the black text flows

beats.n: The last sack is carried up. Pangur Bán threads between ankles, white as the vellum he is not allowed to walk on.
“Tomorrow,” Cillín whispers, “we eat late — fast day or not, the refectory has things to say. And Pangur has opinions about the fish.”

sessions.en: Scriptorium fare — what you like and don't
sessions.hook: Tomorrow the abbot comes to see the book. Your initial must be finished — and the whole house must stand together.

pages.intro: Fast day, but the kitchen still smokes. You pause at the pigment-room door where yesterday's colour words cling to the frame.

beats.n: Bread, milk, water, fish from the Shannon — plain food, eaten in silence broken only by a reader's voice. Murchadh sits with his horn of ink untouched until grace is done.

beats.g: There is bread on the table — literally ‘bread is on the table’

pages.title: Food words you'll meet at every table
paras: The scriptorium runs on simple things:
**Arán** — bread. **Bainne** — milk. **Uisce** — water. **Im** — butter. **Iasc** — fish. **Mil** — honey, when a beekeeper visits.
Notice **tá … ar an mbord** and **tá … ann** — *there is …* — the same *tá* frame as time and tiredness.
pairs: arán — bread  ·  bainne — milk  ·  uisce — water
im — butter  ·  iasc — fish  ·  mil — honey

pages.prompt: Match the word to the refectory plate.

pages.title: An Nóta Gramadaí — *Is maith liom*
paras: Remember Dáire's two verbs? Likes bring the copula back — but sideways:
**Is maith liom an t-arán** — literally *it is good with me, the bread*.
The thing you like is **good** (*maith*); **liom** is *with me*. Irish doesn't say “I like” — it says “good with me.”
Refuse with **Ní maith liom** — not good with me.
pairs: Is maith liom an t-arán. — I like the bread.
Ní maith liom an t-iasc. — I don't like the fish.
Is maith liom bainne. — I like milk.

pages.prompt: How would Cillín say “I like the bread”?

opts.why: Good-with-me: Is maith liom an t-arán.
Likes take the copula is, not tá — even though it feels like a feeling.
The pattern is *good with me* — liom, not *good me*.

pages.prompt: Build: “I don't like the fish.”

pages.place: Ag an mbord — at the table

beats.n: Pangur Bán appears from nowhere — cats respect no fast — and settles beside Cillín's stool. The reader's voice stumbles; someone almost laughs.

beats.g: Do you like the fish? — Connacht shape (Munster often says An maith leat… similarly; Ulster may use different question forms)

pages.cue: Honest answers only — the refectory forgives taste, not lies.

reaction.g: Good man you! — approval of your taste

reaction.n: Pangur Bán looks offended on principle. Fish is his as well.

reaction.s: Tá a fhios agam. Tá sé salach uaireanta.
reaction.g: I know. It is salty sometimes.
reaction.ph: taw iss AH-gum · taw shay SAL-ukh OO-er-an-tuh

reaction.n: He slides the honey bowl toward you instead. **Is maith liom an mil** — he says — and Pangur agrees.

pages.place: Ar ais sa scriptóirium — back in the scriptorium

beats.n: After meals the cat owns the warmest bench. Cillín copies a poem he says an Irish monk once wrote at Reichenau — hunter and scholar, cat and mouse:

beats.s: Tá mé ag lorg rudaí — agus Pangur Bán ag lorg luch.
beats.g: I am searching for things — and Pangur Bán searching for a mouse
beats.ph: taw may eg lur-ug ROO-dee · AH-gus PANG-ur bawn eg lur-ug lukh

beats.n: The poem will outlast the monastery that copied it. But that is tomorrow's museum, not tonight's ink.

pages.context: Say what you like — pick the food that fits your mouth.
pages.g: I like the bread — or swap arán for bainne, mil, whatever is true

pages.prompt: Which line refuses the honey?

opts.why: Ní maith liom — not good with me. The refusal pattern.
That accepts it gladly — Pangur's choice, not a refusal.
That means “I have honey” — possession comes in Chapter 4.

beats.n: Murchadh rolls the great gospel back into its leather cover and looks at the single blank initial still waiting — yours.
“Tomorrow the abbot comes,” he says. “Finish the letter. Finish it together.”

sessions.en: The illuminated letter — unity before winter

pages.intro: The abbot's visit is today. You climb the stairs slowly — every phrase from this week waits on the wall, weathered overnight.

items.en: I like the bread — refectory honesty
I am writing — where the week began

beats.n: Every bench taken. Corcra and gorm laid out like regiments. The initial — your initial — waits on Murchadh's desk: {name}, ready for the first stroke of gold.
Cillín rules a line; another brother grinds; a third reads aloud so the room moves on one breath. Pangur Bán sleeps on the warm vellum scrap — useless, and permitted.

beats.s: Tá muid ag críochnú an leabhair.
beats.g: We are finishing the book — all of us, one manuscript
beats.ph: taw mwidj eg KREE-ukh-noo un LYOW-er

pages.context: Murchadh quizzes as you paint — last review.
pages.prompt: Match the Irish to its meaning.
pairs: Tá sé a deich a chlog

pages.prompt: Build: “I am {name}.” — identity, one last time before the letter.

pages.context: Cillín chalks your progress on a slate — but drops a fada.
pages.prompt: Correct: “Ta me ag scribh.”
pages.hint: Tá, mé, scríobh — three fadas to restore.

pages.context: The abbot's footsteps echo below. Listen —
pages.prompt: Which phrase did Murchadh say?
pages.say: Ní neart go cur le chéile

opts.txt: Ní neart go cur le chéile — no strength without unity
opts.why: The proverb he lives by in the scriptorium — you'll meet it properly in a moment.

opts.txt: Is buaine focal ná toice an tsaoil
opts.why: That was Dáire's stone-yard proverb — words outlasting wealth. Different chapter, same truth.
It may be late — but he said the unity proverb.

beats.n: The abbot enters without ceremony. He walks the benches, touches the vellum, stops at your initial — corcra vine, gorm interlace, the first letter of your name glowing like a small sunrise.
He does not praise. He counts — pages, quires, colours, hands. Then he speaks the house's old verdict:

beats.s: Ní neart go cur le chéile.
beats.g: No strength without unity — many hands, one book
beats.ph: nee nyart guh kur leh KHAY-luh

pages.ga: Ní neart go cur le chéile.
pages.en: There is no strength without unity.
pages.note: The scriptorium's law — one book, many hands. Collected to your museum beside Dáire's words about outlasting wealth.

pages.place: Baile Átha Cliath · an lá inniu

beats.n: The gospel you helped finish did not stay on the Shannon. Centuries later, monks carried it to safety — and today it lives under glass in Dublin: the Book of Kells, pages still shouting corcra and gorm at tourists who queue in the rain.

Pangur Bán survived too — not the cat, but the poem about him, copied in a German monastery by an Irish hand homesick for a white cat and a warm bench. Scholars still argue which monastery. The cat doesn't mind.
Present tense, past glory, living words — you learned the right tense in the right room.

paras: **Caibidil a Trí — Na Lochlannaigh** is next: smoke on the horizon, then a market at the black pool. You'll trade in past tense, and discover you've been speaking Viking Irish your whole life.
You're testing a prototype — after finishing, please tell us: what pulled you back, and what didn't? That answer shapes everything we build next.

visits.frame: The bell has rung for Lauds and the quire waits. Tell him what you're doing at the bench.
He asks why you're here so early. You're at work — say it.
He holds up fingers — seven quires left before winter. Name the number.
The sun is at mid-morning. He wants the hour spoken properly.
visits.answer: Tá sé a sé a chlog

visits.frame: He lifts the lichen cake — the colour that costs more than gold. Name it.
The honey bowl passes. Pangur watches. Admit you like it.
He stands before the finished book — many hands, one gospel. Give him the house proverb.
visits.answer: Ní neart go cur le chéile
